A1.justification: Both PDFs describe BEYOND DIALOGUE, with matching methods, datasets, and experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison despite extensive reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original role-playing evaluations, alignment experiments, ablations, dialogue-extraction measurements, and human verification results.

after.justification: V6 retains these empirical results and adds human preference comparisons, evaluation-format experiments, and results from a second LLM judge.

M1.justification: The extraction, CSERP alignment, profile adjustment, and supervised training procedures remain substantively unchanged, including the objective and 1:5:4 data mixture. The coarse/refined terminology and expanded reasoning explanation clarify existing components; the appendix prompt templates are substantively identical.

E1.justification: Both use the same Chinese-English coverage: 123 novels/scripts, 311 roles, 3,552 dialogues, and 23,247 turns, alongside NaturalConv and DailyDialog. Added human and judge-validation experiments assess the existing role-playing and profile-alignment tasks.

E2.justification: The role-playing, alignment, and extraction baseline sets are retained. V6 Appendix B.1 adds subjective scoring and objective scoring without chain-of-thought as comparison methods for evaluating the proposed assessment approach.

E3.justification: V6 replaces average CSERP summaries in role-playing and ablation results with Qualification Rate, requiring scores above 60 in every dimension. It adds majority-vote human preferences against GPT-4o, Claude-3-Opus judging, and a 50-instance evaluation-format experiment. Appendix D retains the original seen/unseen-role split; the main text's 'all new roles' wording is inconsistent and does not establish a changed split.

E4.justification: V6 adds controlled subjective/objective and reasoning-prompt comparisons (Appendix B.1), validation across judges (B.2), and dataset profile-misalignment analysis (A.3). The original five task-removal ablations and alignment cases remain; merged dialogue figures largely redisplay existing cases.

E5.justification: Both already report SEMs and t-tests. V6 adds three repeated evaluations per condition in the 50-instance experiment, Krippendorff's alpha, and additional human-agreement statistics including Cohen's kappa. Conversely, Table 12 removes the uncertainty estimates previously accompanying validity and cosine similarity in v1 Table 9. These additions concern evaluation reliability, not additional training seeds.

E6.justification: The original main-table component scores, alignment results, and per-dimension ablation results are unchanged. V6 adds Qualification Rates, human win rates of 71.00% for fully trained Qwen2 and 69.33% for fully trained Mistral against GPT-4o, Claude evaluations, and agreement results. HPD reporting replaces separate character/style bias percentages with an 83.2% any-dimension statistic, rather than a comparable performance change.

T1.justification: V6 adds an explicit mathematical definition of the joint unaligned ratio in Appendix A.3 and defines the threshold-based Qualification Rate. The training objective is unchanged, and neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain identifying profile-dialogue bias, introducing sentence-level alignment training, and providing automated objective evaluation. Claims of improved profile adherence and superiority to most general and specialized baselines retain their scope. The self-evaluation discussion remains in the alignment-results section.

C2.justification: V6 explicitly discusses limitations involving evolving profiles, autonomous adaptation of global profiles, multi-party dialogue, and inherited safety constraints. It adds an interpretation of judge differences as possible self-preference. Ablation emphasis shifts from Character/Style to Character/Personality when interpreted through Qualification Rate.

D1.justification: V6 adds annotation recruitment and pilot-timing information plus explicit Apache 2.0 and CC BY-NC 4.0 licensing terms. It removes v1's GPU, memory, and operating-system disclosure. Training and inference hyperparameters, substantive prompt templates, and the repository link remain available.

R1.justification: V6 adds ERAbaL and OpenCharacter, explicitly contrasts sentence-level alignment with loosely profile-guided generation, and adds references supporting the additional judge. The main related-work taxonomy and novelty positioning remain stable; publication and citation-format updates are largely bibliographic.

P1.justification: V6 substantially edits and reorganizes the exposition, introduces numbered sections and appendices, repairs missing section references, and separates coarse construction from profile refinement. It rewrites several methodological and results passages and condenses the lengthy cost discussion.

P2.justification: The framework diagrams are reordered and revised; result tables gain Qualification Rate, human preferences, and color shading; Figure 4 changes its aggregate-score panel. V6 adds evaluation and cost tables, expands the human-verification table, merges model-specific dialogue figures, and compacts the prompt layouts.

improvement.justification: V1's central model comparisons relied on GPT-4o judging, while the claimed stability advantage of objective evaluation lacked a controlled comparison. V6 adds human preferences, a second judge, and repeated evaluation-format controls (Tables 2, 8–9, and 11), substantially strengthening evidence for the models and evaluation pipeline. Explicit limitations and repaired organization also improve interpretability. Lost hardware details, removed uncertainty estimates, and inconsistent role-split wording are drawbacks, but the added validation provides a substantial net improvement.
